source_span: the composite PMI unexpectedly hit a 5-year high of 58.4 in September (vs. 55.3 expected). So that played into the narrative of resilient growth, which in turn would enable the Fed to keep hiking rates
source_chain: Composite PMI beats hard (58.4 vs 55.3) therefore the resilient-growth narrative lets the Fed keep hiking therefore Fed-hike pricing jumps (Oct to 71%, year-end to 37bps) and the 10yr sells off to a post-2007 high of 5.11%, worsened by a weak 5yr auction. DB gives no discrete invalidation level; it argues the repricing continues because markets historically underestimate hikes at the outset (companion note, 'The hawkish risk: How markets keep underestimating the scale of rate hikes').
pulse_chain: PMI beat (58.4 vs 55.3, DB) therefore bond market deletes cuts and prices hikes (10yr to 5.11%/5.16%, 37bp priced, Oct 71%) therefore equities are pressured because rate-cut-dependent valuations break at this yield level, with the 5yr auction tail (JPM) as the mechanical extension. Pulse then adds its own invalidation: the Sep 30 growth/inflation reports are 'the first hard test' of whether the PMI surge is real or a 'one-month survey artifact,' and JPMorgan's 5.5% fair-value level 'settles whether this is an overshoot to buy or a repricing to respect,' with the wide 5yr auction offered as 'the tell' that JPM's buy-the-dip case isn't ready yet.
why: The PMI-to-hawkish-repricing-to-selloff chain is faithfully carried from the DB note, but the pulse's invalidation ('Sept 30 data is the hard test of whether September was an artifact,' and the auction as 'the tell' that settles JPM's 5.5% buy call) is not argued by any source file in the list — JPM's own stated buy triggers are yields nearing fair value, valuation cushion, and geopolitical de-escalation, not an upcoming data print, so the pulse substitutes its own invented resolving condition for the one JPM actually gives.
